A0003.title: Cloud-Side Anti-Crawling
A0003.definition: Identifying and restricting crawler requests on the server side based on terminal request characteristics and access frequency.
A0003.description: Also known as cloud-side crawler identification. Broadly speaking, any capability for human-machine identification or automated request detection falls under the scope of crawler identification. Here we use a narrow definition: the ability to identify high-frequency automated requests on the server side based on terminal request characteristics, user identity, and access frequency. Terminal request characteristics include but are not limited to: device fingerprinting and terminal tracking (A0021), request IP and HTTP header information, etc. Terminal request characteristics combined with user identity enable unique identification of the requesting endpoint; combined with server-side algorithms and rate/count limits per unit time, this enables identification and restriction of high-frequency automated requests. For unauthenticated or unverified requests, cloud-side anti-crawling sets resource-access thresholds (such as mandatory login, limiting the type and volume of data accessible without login) to shrink the attack surface and concentrate defensive resources.
A0003.limitation: Detection depends on signals that uniquely identify the requester, establish identity, and measure request frequency. Attackers can rotate IP addresses and user agents, forge device fingerprints, distribute requests across bulk accounts, or crawl slowly to bypass rate thresholds. Legitimate automation such as search-engine crawlers may also be falsely blocked. Detection latency makes this control less effective against instantaneous actions such as last-second bidding and auction sniping, so it should be combined with client validation and business-process restrictions.
